segments.text: One insurance claim. One AI agent. We'll ask it the same question twice: first on the insurer's data as it is today, and then on AI-ready data.

First, the domain in plain words. A car is damaged in an accident on the twelfth of October. The owner files a claim for four point two lakh rupees. The insurer checks the policy: was the car covered, and for what, on the day of the accident? It reads the evidence: the police report, called an FIR, the garage's invoice, and the surveyor's report. Then it decides: pay quickly, which insurers call fast-track, or send it to investigators. Three terms you'll hear. A zero-dep add-on: extra cover that only counts if it was bought before the accident. Severity band B2: major repair. And a fraud ring: many claims quietly sharing the same garage and phone. This is the question we give the agent.

Here's what we built. The insurer's data lives in a claims database, a policy system, a CRM, a spreadsheet and uploaded PDFs. Dagster, a data pipeline tool, runs every step and checks it. Bronze keeps raw copies of every source. Silver cleans them: one claim ID, one person instead of two, the policy's full history, and documents with owners and versions. Rows that fail a check are held back, not passed on. Gold holds features and signals, like the fraud score. It all lands in a lakehouse: Apache Iceberg tables, queried with DuckDB.

Three more stores are filled from there. Meaning: the teams write the glossary, column meanings and privacy rules as files; the pipeline adds every table from the lakehouse; and an AI model drafts meanings nobody wrote yet, flagged for review. All of it goes into OpenMetadata, the data catalog. Documents: the PDFs are read, split by section, and stored in Qdrant, so passages can be found by meaning and cited. Connections: every mention of a garage, a phone or a person, in tables and in documents, is resolved into one entity and linked, with evidence, in Neo4j, a graph database. And the graph is linked back to the catalog.

The agent never touches these databases directly. It talks to one governed gateway: the unified discovery plane, also available over MCP. The plane offers tools like policy terms, document search and graph links. It masks personal data by role, records every call, and will not pay anything without a person.

Now the same question, to two agents side by side, using the same model. On the left, the agent-first build, wired straight to the systems the insurer already has. On the right, the same agent, working through the discovery plane. Each line is one tool call, described in plain words.

Left: fast-track, four lakh seven thousand rupees, payout queued. It never saw a risk, because it could not see the evidence. Right: hold, and route to investigators. Let's step through how the right side got there.

First, the policy as it stood on the accident day. The zero-dep add-on was added the day after, so it does not apply. The pipeline rebuilt that history from the policy system's audit log. Here, in Dagster, are the two versions of the policy.

Next, meaning. Instead of guessing what cryptic columns mean, the agent read them from the catalog. This is OpenMetadata. Every table in the lakehouse is listed here. Open one, and each column has a plain meaning, an owner, and tags for personal data. The glossary holds owned definitions: severity band B2 means major repair.

Then the evidence. It searched the documents by meaning, and found page two of the police report: the car went to FixIt Motors. In Qdrant, every passage is stored with its document, page and section. That's what makes it citable.
Along the way, the plane masked over thirty personal details about other people, before they ever reached the model.

Then the connections. The knowledge graph showed five other claims within thirty days, with the same garage and the same contact phone. In Neo4j you can see the ring: six claims, one garage, one phone, every link backed by a page in a document.
Finally, the fraud score, computed once by the pipeline using those graph links: zero point eight two. The insurer's live fraud API, which can't see the graph, says zero point zero two.
So it holds the claim and routes it to investigators, with the evidence attached. A person makes the call.

Data doesn't stay ready by itself. A week later, a new claim arrives with a police report written as a letter. A Dagster job asks a language model to read it. The model finds the garage and the phone, with exact quotes, and rules check every quote before the graph is updated. The ring grows to seven claims, and investigators are alerted.
Before you make your AI smarter, make your data ready.
